It also remembers that the Empire appears not only to historians but to ordinary people who know it in one way or another—and even to the people who once actually lived within it.
When the phenomenologist speaks of the Empire, then, he speaks not of the Empire itself but of its appearance: both of how it appears and of the person to whom it appears.

The historian, of course, also deals with the people who lived in the Roman Empire. But he describes them as they appear to him, not as they appeared to themselves, and usually not as the Empire to which they belonged appeared to them.
In other words, he leaves aside their consciousness of themselves—their self-consciousness.
In any case, he does not discuss the cognition through which they experienced and understood their own Empire.
History in the narrow sense—the history of social and political reality—therefore leaves aside both consciousness and cognition.
What about the so-called history of ideas: the history of worldviews, religions, sciences, or even philosophy?
Here the historian does introduce “consciousness,” but he still leaves aside “cognition”—precisely what primarily concerns psychology.
Suppose a historian studies the Catholic worldview of the thirteenth century and the physics of the seventeenth.

He will describe not only their “appearance”—while naturally imagining that he is describing the things themselves—not only the content of that worldview and that physics, but also the “consciousness” of the thirteenth- and seventeenth-century people who created them.
Even so, he will not discuss their cognition in the sense of asking how, and through what “psychological means,” they produced these forms of thought.
The same applies to the historian of philosophy.

When discussing Plato, for example, the historian will speak about the content of Plato’s philosophy and about Plato himself, but not about Plato’s “cognition”—the psychological means through which Plato developed his philosophy.
The phenomenologist, like the psychologist, is primarily interested in precisely this cognition.
His aim, after all, is to make genuine philosophical knowledge possible.

History matters to Phenomenology only insofar as it is the history of this knowledge: the history of human cognition that eventually led to phenomenological knowledge and, through phenomenological knowledge, to philosophical knowledge—that is, ultimately, to perfect knowledge, wisdom, or omniscience.
In this sense, as I have already said, Phenomenology is above all a theory of knowledge: a science or theory of cognition. If one wishes, it can therefore also be called a kind of psychology.

But unlike ordinary theories of knowledge and ordinary psychology, Phenomenology studies concrete cognition. This cognition is inseparably connected not only with its content—the appearances or phenomena—but also with the real consciousness in which that content occurs: with the actual human being.
For this reason, it is better to call Phenomenology an anthropology.
And because concrete human cognition is essentially historical, phenomenological anthropology—or phenomenological theory of knowledge—is historical too.
Still, if we want to distinguish Phenomenology from history, it is better to call this phenomenological anthropology or theory of knowledge dialectical rather than merely “historical.”
For, as we will see again, the development and existence of concrete cognition and concrete consciousness—that is, of human beings—is not only historical in the ordinary sense. It is dialectical.
In terms of its subject matter or object, then, Phenomenology can be defined as a “dialectical anthropology.”

Calling it an “anthropology” emphasizes that it is first and foremost a theory of knowledge or psychology. But it also tells us how this theory of knowledge and psychology differs from its ordinary scientific forms: it deals not with abstract cognition or “consciousness in general,” but with the concrete cognition and consciousness of a human being.

The word “dialectical,” meanwhile, emphasizes its historical character. The cognition and consciousness of the human being studied by Phenomenology are not eternal and unchanging. They develop through time according to definite laws.

We therefore call phenomenological anthropology dialectical rather than merely historical, partly to distinguish it from ordinary scholarly history and partly to indicate that the laws governing the development of human consciousness are dialectical.
But in defining Phenomenology as a “dialectical anthropology,” we must not forget that it is first and foremost Phenomenology: a philosophical science of phenomena or “appearances.”

In other words, unlike the dialectical anthropology that forms part of Cosmology, Phenomenology does not describe the real existence of human beings themselves within the natural world—their specifically human existence together with their material or bodily existence.
It describes the human being as phenomenon or appearance: the human being as he appears to himself throughout the historical development of humanity.
And because a human being appears to himself through a cognition of himself, while a consciousness that knows itself is self-consciousness, we can give Phenomenology a still more precise definition.
As phenomeno-logy, it is a philosophical description of the development of self-consciousness—or, if one prefers, the dialectical history of self-consciousness.
This is obviously true when Phenomenology describes the “appearance” of a human being and of the human world to a human being.
But it remains true even when Phenomenology deals with the natural world.
For it does not discuss the natural world itself. It discusses its “appearance”: the content of a human consciousness directed toward the natural world.

And human consciousness is always also self-consciousness. A human being is conscious not only of what he is conscious of, but also of the fact that he is conscious, and that he himself is the one who is conscious.
Ultimately, therefore, what the phenomenologist describes is self-consciousness.
But we must again remember that this is concrete self-consciousness: human self-consciousness, which means historical self-consciousness.
Phenomenology studies the history of self-consciousness, or self-consciousness in its historical development.

Phenomenology is therefore the philosophical and dialectical history of self-consciousness: “history,” as against psychology and the ordinary theory of knowledge; “of self-consciousness,” as against ordinary history.
It describes the historical—and therefore dialectical—development or becoming of human self-consciousness.

It begins with the “birth” of self-consciousness, with its “simplest” form: the moment when a human being first said “I”—when a human being first began to speak about himself, to refer to himself, and therefore to know himself and become conscious of himself.
It ends with the appearance of complete self-consciousness: a form that is therefore the “last” one, because its development can go no further.
This complete self-consciousness is that of the philosopher—or more exactly, the sage.

And because philosophical self-consciousness is also, for that very reason, the self-consciousness of the phenomenologist, we can say that the phenomenologist brings the history of self-consciousness to an end by describing his own self-consciousness.

As we will see, this self-consciousness is phenomenological—which means philosophical, and therefore complete, final, and definitive—because it is, so to speak, the sum of all the forms of self-consciousness described in Phenomenology, all of which appear as possible types of self-consciousness in general.

The phenomenologist can continue describing the historical development of self-consciousness only so long as his own self-consciousness is broader than the forms he describes—only so long as his description allows him to see that those earlier forms are still incomplete and that their development has therefore not yet finished.
But if the phenomenologist’s own self-consciousness is complete, this means that he “appears” to himself exactly as he really is.
At that point he no longer appears to himself as a phenomenologist. He is given to himself as a philosopher.

And once he becomes a philosopher, he can move beyond describing “appearances.” He can describe existing reality itself, including himself as something that really exists, and the being that underlies reality—including, of course, his own existence.
Phenomenology therefore ends, so to speak, where “appearances” and the forms of cognition and consciousness corresponding to them come to an end.
Phenomenology ends where knowledge of the things themselves begins.

In other words, Phenomenology describes all the incomplete forms of “consciousness” that have some cognition of “phenomena” without understanding that they are phenomena—that is, without understanding how their cognition takes place and who is doing the cognizing.

In this sense Phenomenology is genuinely a complete phenomenology: a universal description that exhausts every possible form of “appearance”, together with every corresponding form of cognition and consciousness—that is, ultimately, every form of self-consciousness.
Phenomenology therefore gives an exhaustive description of all phenomena that have existed or do exist: all the ways in which the world and humanity appear to human beings.
In doing so, it describes every type of human self-consciousness.

And because it describes self-consciousness phenomenologically—that is, philosophically and therefore concretely—it also describes every type of human existence, insofar as that existence is conscious.

More exactly, it describes every type of human existence insofar as human beings become conscious of it: insofar as that existence “appears” through a corresponding form of cognition, through the “experience” of the consciousness of the human beings who actually embody that type of existence.

Phenomenology continues doing this for as long as there remains a difference between an existence itself and its “appearance”—for as long as the self-consciousness of that existence remains incomplete.
Or, what amounts to the same thing, it continues for as long as the phenomenologist can see more in a form of existence than the corresponding consciousness can say about itself.
Those consciousnesses believe they are saying everything that can be said about their existence. They therefore forget that what they are describing is an “appearance,” not existence itself.

Phenomenology passes through all these forms of human existence until it finally reaches philosophical, and therefore phenomenological, existence—the existence of its own author, who will also become the author of the future philosophical system.
At that point Phenomenology fully comprehends its author’s self-consciousness, and his existence therefore ceases to be merely an “appearance.”
So Phenomenology describes every type of human existence insofar as it appears as a phenomenon.

And because these forms of existence are conscious, while consciousness includes a kind of “cognitive experience,” Phenomenology describes every type of human experience—experience both of oneself and of the world—from the “first” and “simplest” form all the way to phenomenological, and therefore philosophical, experience.

In this sense, it describes the course of education or formation (Erfahrung) undergone by human consciousness: the path along which consciousness and cognition have travelled before reaching the experience expressed in a Phenomenology that describes precisely the path that led to itself.
The “cognitive experience” described in Phenomenology makes different aspects of existence—the world and humanity—“appear” to human consciousness.
A later consciousness “remembers” the earlier experience and adds a new one to it. The aspect of existence that appears therefore becomes progressively broader and deeper.
The “last” experience gathers up all the earlier ones. By bringing together all the aspects of existence, it arrives at a complete cognition of reality and thereby turns into perfect knowledge.
The consciousness possessing this knowledge has become philosophical.
But this “summing up” of experiences and of the aspects revealed through them is nothing other than the whole of the Phenomenology that describes them.

We can therefore say that consciousness becomes philosophical—that is, capable of omniscience and of rising to Cosmology and Ontology—precisely because it has first become phenomenological consciousness.

And it becomes phenomenological only after it has described every form of experience and every form of consciousness—that is, all non-phenomenological or pre-phenomenological forms of self-consciousness.

Once the phenomenologist has described all the appearances of the world and humanity to human beings, while also counting himself among those appearances, he cannot continue describing appearances because no new ones remain.

If he wants to go further, he must stop describing “appearance” and begin describing existence itself, together with the being that underlies it—the existence that has now become “given” to him through his phenomenological description of every appearance.
In short, he must write a systematic Philosophy.
Phenomenology therefore does more than make philosophy genuinely possible. In principle, it also proves philosophy to be true.

It does so by showing that the philosopher’s self-consciousness is complete: his experience of his object includes not only the object but also his experience of cognition itself and of himself as philosopher.

His cognition therefore ceases to be an “opinion” and becomes genuine “knowledge.” It becomes experience not merely of the “appearances” or isolated “aspects” of existence, but knowledge of existence itself taken as a whole—that is, taken concretely.

Of course, everything just said is true only if Phenomenology really does describe all the types of “experience” or “self-consciousness” that are possible in principle—or, where they are not final types, all those that have actually existed by the time Phenomenology itself emerges.
In other words, it must describe every type of conscious human existence.
The only thing that can guarantee this completeness is knowledge of the law governing the development of human existence and determining the stages—or types—through which it passes.
As we will see, and as we already know, this law is called dialectic. This is why it matters that Phenomenology is a dialectical science.

By knowing and demonstrating this dialectic, Phenomenology can begin with the “simplest” consciousness or self-consciousness—the simplest form of conscious existence—and show how and why it must eventually pass into the next form, then the next, and so on.
Phenomenology can therefore be certain that it has omitted no stage and no type of human existence.
It can also be certain that it has exhausted them all.
That is why it finally arrives at itself and can obviously go no further.

On the one hand, it arrives at the self-consciousness—or form of existence—of its own author, whose existence culminates in writing the Phenomenology. On the other hand, it then describes that very existence.
At this point Phenomenology would simply have to repeat itself, since the phenomenologist’s form of existence consists in writing the Phenomenology itself.

Phenomenology therefore knows that it has described all the types of self-consciousness or conscious human existence that are either possible in general or historically realized by the time it appears.
And this knowledge allows it to select from the material supplied by history.
